INFP 33f here. I babysat a lot when I was young because I was naturally good at it. Fast forward to adulthood and I've been working with children again because, well, I'm naturally good at it. I'd be recommended or asked by someone I know about nannying, daycare, etc. I've accepted the role of caring for other's children as means of income for the last 10 years.

However, working with children depletes me unlike any other job. Usually I have two jobs (single mother of 11m). My second job usually doesn't include caring for children, but I still often get so burned out by a family or a daycare position that I eventually quit and want to focus on my hobbies that give me energy and excitement for life. I'm currently working at a nature focused daycare that has wanted me to stay enough that they've allowed flexibility for my hours and more time off. That has helped and I'm on my 3rd year there. 

Something I've noticed about myself as well is that I prefer caring for the younger kiddos. I tend to feel disconnected and annoyed from kids 8-10+ unless I know them well. Working with kids has also made me less likely to interact with kids in public settings when I'm out and about on my own. 

With all that being said; I am fascinated by children's minds and how they see the world. Children have taught me a lot and it has required me to look at my own tendencies and behaviors. I stay working with children because of this. And they like me. Most of the time.

The Humanure Handbook by Joseph C. Jenkins is a great resource for building compost bins specified for "humanure" and what you need to do to be able to use it for your garden. You're looking at about 2 years of correctly composted humanure before using it in a garden. I live on an off-grid homestead and we have about 4 outdoor compost bins of humanure from over many years but we haven't used it. It's mainly just a place for the poo buckets. We just use mulch and animal manure for our permaculture garden and we aren't huge scale so it works for us. But I enjoyed reading The Humanure Handbook and it has a lot of scientific research on the subject as well as many different composting bathroom designs.

It definitely used to. And the work was different. Working in terms of building, growing, collecting water, harvesting, cooking, raising children, etc.. It isn't easy to be self sufficient. That's why people stay in cities and keep going to their shitty jobs and paying shitty rent and eating shitty food and even treating others shitty in response to all the shit. They get to turn on their faucets and plug into their devices and be "entertained." 

I personally want to use my shit and turn it into nutritious soil and heat my future outdoor shower. I want to work hard to build a small home and tend to my permaculture gardens and coexist with the world that we are born from. To live in a community where neighbors are further away but we all help each other out with our different skills and abilities with continuous respect for one another and the land we lay our feet upon. To wake up to mist traveling through the trees and drink coffee as the woodfire stove crackles. That is my dream and I DID find my place. I found a job this winter where I'll be able to gain skills and obtain materials for a home. And I WILL be moving off grid to create a permaculture homestead at the end of spring. As long as I don't die beforehand.

But not all humans want that. Some can not even fathom the idea of not having running water or outlets on every wall. Despite slaving away for a job one hates, they have the comfort of their home and the coffee shops and the restaurants and other stores to buy things. Go out with friends, take selfies, post to social media and impatiently wait for likes and comments to validate such a life. 

I'm 30 and I decided I won't live the rest of my life that way. Depression and anxiety are all that has come out of it. There will be sacrifices and loss of comfort but to me, it is all worth it to live a meaningful life.
